passages.t: ‘Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up’
passages.happening:
Paul takes up the next question from the Corinthians' letter. “Now about food sacrificed to idols: We know that we all have knowledge. Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up” (verse 1).

“The one who thinks he knows something does not yet know as he ought to know” (verse 2).

“But the one who loves God is known by God” (verse 3).
passages.hearers:
Almost every Greek and Roman city was full of temples, and Corinth had many: to Apollo, to Aphrodite, to the healing god Asclepius, and others. When an animal was offered to a god, part of it was burned on the altar and much of the meat was eaten. Some was eaten at feasts in the temple's own dining rooms. Some was sold in the market. At Corinth the sanctuary of Asclepius had dining rooms where such meals were held. An invitation to a dinner ‘at the table of the lord Sarapis’, another god, survives on a papyrus from Egypt.

So the question was not small. Meals at temples were part of ordinary life: birthdays, weddings, business dinners, the gatherings of trade guilds, city festivals. For a believer of some standing, refusing to go could cost friends, business and honour. For poorer believers, meat was rare except at festivals, when it came from the sacrifices, so meat itself was bound up with the gods.

Many translators think ‘We know that we all have knowledge’ quotes the Corinthians' own letter. The Berean Standard Bible prints it without quotation marks; this is a judgment translators make. Some Corinthians were sure they knew better than to worry: idols are nothing, so eating is nothing.

Paul agrees with what they know. But he puts something above it. ‘Puffs up’ is physioō, to inflate, the word for the church's pride all through this letter. ‘Builds up’ is oikodomeō, to build a house. Knowledge on its own swells the one who has it. Love builds up the other person.

Verse 3 turns the whole matter round. What matters most is not what you know about God, but that God knows you.
passages.ot:
In the Old Testament, to be ‘known’ by God means to be chosen and cared for by him. God says through Hosea, “you know no God but Me, for there is no Savior besides Me” (Hosea 13:4), and in Exodus, when Israel suffered in Egypt, “God saw the Israelites and took notice” (Exodus 2:25). Paul says the same in another letter: “now that you know God, or rather are known by God” (Galatians 4:9).

Jeremiah set knowing God above every other kind of knowing. The one who boasts should boast in this: “that he understands and knows Me, that I am the LORD” (Jeremiah 9:24). Paul quoted that verse in 1:31.
passages.asks: Paul says knowledge without love swells a person up. Ask when being right has mattered more to you than the person in front of you. And ask what you rest your standing with God on: what you know about him, or the fact that he knows you.

passages.t: ‘One God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ’
passages.happening:
Paul comes back to the question. “So about eating food sacrificed to idols: We know that an idol is nothing at all in the world, and that there is no God but one” (verse 4).

There are, it is true, many beings called gods, in heaven and on earth, “as there are many so-called gods and lords” (verse 5).

Then he says, “yet for us there is but one God, the Father, from whom all things came and for whom we exist. And there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things came and through whom we exist” (verse 6).
passages.hearers:
‘An idol is nothing at all in the world’ and ‘there is no God but one’ may again be the Corinthians' own words, which Paul accepts. Every Jew believed them. The Corinthians who ate in temples used them as their reason: if the gods are not real, a temple dinner is just dinner.

‘So-called gods and lords’ would have rung true in Corinth. The city honoured many gods in its temples. The emperors were honoured as divine in the eastern cities, and ‘lord’, kyrios, was a title for a ruler as well as a master. Paul does not deny that people bowed to these beings. He says that, for believers, there is one God and one Lord.

Then comes verse 6, one of the most important sentences Paul ever wrote. Every Jew knew Israel's great confession of faith, the Shema, named for its first word, ‘Hear’: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). It was recited in Jewish prayer. In the Greek translation of the Old Testament, the words ‘God’ and ‘Lord’ both appear in it.

Paul takes that confession and divides it, without breaking it. ‘One God’ he applies to the Father. ‘One Lord’ he applies to Jesus Christ. And he says that all things came ‘through’ Jesus, which means Jesus was there at the making of the world. Paul does not add Jesus as a second god beside the one God. He places Jesus inside Israel's confession of the one God.

Paul wrote this about twenty to twenty-five years after the crucifixion. So this is not a late idea. It is one of the earliest and highest statements about Christ in the whole New Testament.
passages.ot:
The confession behind verse 6 is the Shema: “Hear, O Israel: The LORD our God, the LORD is One” (Deuteronomy 6:4). Jesus himself called it the most important commandment (Mark 12:29).

The Old Testament says again and again that there is one God and the idols are nothing. “For all the gods of the nations are idols, but it is the LORD who made the heavens” (Psalm 96:5). “I am the first and I am the last, and there is no God but Me” (Isaiah 44:6). Jeremiah mocks idols as scarecrows that cannot speak or walk (Jeremiah 10:5). And God is “God of gods and Lord of lords” (Deuteronomy 10:17).

‘Through whom all things came’ echoes what the Old Testament says of God's word and wisdom at creation. “By the word of the LORD the heavens were made” (Psalm 33:6). “The LORD founded the earth by wisdom” (Proverbs 3:19). Paul says that what was done through God's word and wisdom was done through Jesus Christ.
passages.hard:
What does verse 6 say about who Jesus is?

It says something very high, and these notes say so plainly. Paul, a Jew who prayed the Shema, takes Israel's confession of the one God and places Jesus within it. The Father is the ‘one God’, from whom all things came. Jesus Christ is the ‘one Lord’, through whom all things came. To share in the making of all things is to stand on God's side of the line between Creator and creation.

Many scholars, among them Richard Bauckham in Jesus and the God of Israel (2008), read the verse this way: Paul has placed Jesus inside the one God's own confession. Some scholars read it more modestly, and that debate is real. But the church has always confessed what this verse points to. Jesus Christ is truly God and truly man. The Nicene Creed, which the great churches share, uses the same pairing: it confesses one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things were made. That belongs to the confessional floor of the Christian faith. It is confessed here, not put to a vote.

Other New Testament writers say the same. “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1:1). “Through Him all things were made” (John 1:3).

How can there be one God, and yet the Father and Jesus each be confessed as God? That is the question the doctrine of the Trinity answers. The site's Honest Answer, ‘How can God be three and one?’, sets out the case against it at full strength and what the creeds claim.
passages.asks: In a city full of gods and lords, Paul said there is one God and one Lord. Ask what ‘lords’ make claims on your life today: money, a nation, a party, success, a person's approval. Then ask what it would mean, this week, to confess with Paul that for you there is ‘one Lord, Jesus Christ’.

passages.t: The weak conscience, and giving up a right
passages.happening:
“But not everyone has this knowledge” (verse 7). Some believers were so used to idols that when they eat such food they still feel it as food offered to an idol. “And since their conscience is weak, it is defiled” (verse 7).

“But food does not bring us closer to God: We are no worse if we do not eat, and no better if we do” (verse 8).

“Be careful, however, that your freedom does not become a stumbling block to the weak” (verse 9). If someone with a weak conscience sees you, who know better, eating in an idol's temple, will he not be encouraged to eat food offered to idols (verse 10)?

“So this weak brother, for whom Christ died, is destroyed by your knowledge” (verse 11). Sinning against your brothers in this way, and wounding their weak conscience, “you sin against Christ” (verse 12).

Paul ends with his own choice. “Therefore, if what I eat causes my brother to stumble, I will never eat meat again, so that I will not cause him to stumble” (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
The ‘weak’ here are not weak in will or in faith in general. They are believers, probably recent converts from the worship of the gods, who could not yet eat such meat without feeling they were joining in that worship again. Their old life was too close.

Conscience, in Greek syneidēsis, is the inner sense that judges your own actions. To act against your conscience, even when it is mistaken, harms you. You learn to ignore the voice that tells you what is wrong.

Picture the scene in verse 10. A believer who knows that idols are nothing reclines at a dinner in a temple dining room. A newer believer, who used to worship that god, sees him there. He reasons: if he can, so can I. And he goes back into the temple, but with a troubled heart, as if worshipping again. The ‘knowledge’ of the first has led the second back toward the life Christ rescued him from.

Paul does not settle this by saying who is right about idols. He agrees with the ones who know. But he says the weak brother is someone ‘for whom Christ died’. Christ gave his life for him. Can you not give up a meal?

Verse 13 is not a new law against meat. It is Paul's own choice, said with force: he would rather never eat meat again than make a brother fall. The next chapter will show Paul giving up many of his rights in the same way. And in chapter 10 he will add a harder word about actually eating in temples.

The site's notes on Romans 14 take up the same question of the weak and the strong in the church at Rome, and say more.
passages.ot:
The law of Moses already forbade putting something in another's way that would make them fall. “You must not curse the deaf or place a stumbling block before the blind, but you shall fear your God” (Leviticus 19:14).

Israel's history held warnings about eating at the gods' feasts. In the wilderness, the people of Moab “invited them to the sacrifices for their gods. And the people ate and bowed down to these gods” (Numbers 25:2). The law warned that the nations “will invite you, and you will eat their sacrifices” (Exodus 34:15). In Babylon, Daniel “made up his mind that he would not defile himself with the king’s food” (Daniel 1:8).

The teaching of Jesus stands behind ‘stumbling block’. He warned, “if anyone causes one of these little ones who believe in Me to stumble, it would be better for him to have a large millstone hung around his neck” (Matthew 18:6).
passages.hard:
Does this passage mean that anyone who disapproves of something can stop others from doing it? Christians have sometimes read it that way, and it can be misused.

Paul's ‘weak’ believer is not simply someone who dislikes what others do. He is someone who may be drawn back into what he believes is sin, against his own conscience, by another's example, and so be ‘destroyed’ (verse 11). The concern is a person's faith, not someone's taste. Paul writes the same in Romans: “It is better not to eat meat or drink wine or to do anything to cause your brother to stumble” (Romans 14:21). The notes on Romans 14 say more.

Christians differ on where conscience ends and the gospel begins. All agree that no one should be pushed to act against their conscience, and that love gives up rights for others. Paul himself would not give way when someone tried to make a rule binding on everyone and so change the gospel (Galatians 2:3-5). Here the question is different: whether to give up your freedom for the good of a weaker brother or sister. Paul says yes.
passages.asks: Paul measures freedom by what it does to others. Ask whether there is something you are free to do that may be harming someone whose faith is fragile. Then ask what it would cost you to give it up, and compare that with what Christ gave for that person.
